title: Die Rose
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 203. Text from Wikisource („Die Rose (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: A brief tale told entirely in Low German (Plattdeutsch), of a poor widow whose younger child goes into the forest each day to fetch wood, and is helped there, unseen by the mother, by a beautiful child who then vanishes. The stranger leaves behind a rose with a promise to return when it blooms; when the rose opens one morning, it is the widow's own child who is found dead in bed, lying quite peacefully.

sentences.t: Et was mal eine arme Frugge, de hadde twei Kinner; dat jungeste moste olle Dage in en Wald gohn un langen (holen) Holt.
sentences.l: There was once a poor woman, who had two children; the younger one had to go every day into a wood and fetch (get) wood.
sentences.i: There was once a poor woman who had two children; the younger one had to go every day into a wood to fetch firewood.
sentences.n: This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north — expect it throughout, and see the glossary for High German equivalents. Sound-swaps to watch for from the first line: “et” = es, “de” = die, “un” = und, “to” = zu, “dat” = das. “Frugge” = Frau; “Kinner” = Kinder; “twei” = zwei; “gohn” = gehen. “olle Dage” is the Low German phrase for “alle Tage” (every day) — olle here is “alle,” not “alte.” “Holt” is the noun “Holz” (wood), not the imperative of halten. The parenthesis “(holen)” is the Grimms’ own inline gloss on “langen” for a High German reader — reproduced in t exactly; round brackets in the text are Grimm’s, square brackets are the editor’s.

sentences.t: Asset nu mal ganz wiet söken geit, kam so en klein Kind, dat was awerst ganz wacker, to em und holp (half) flietig Holt lesen un drog et auck bis für dat Hus;
sentences.l: As it now once was going quite far to seek, there came such a small child — but it was quite bright and lively — to her, and helped (half) diligently to gather wood, and carried it as well right up to the house;
sentences.i: Once, when she was going quite a way off to search, a small child came up to her — a wide-awake, spirited one — and helped her diligently to gather wood, and carried it too right up to the house;
sentences.n: “Asset” is “As et” written as one word — “als es,” when it. “söken” = suchen; “geit” = geht. “awerst” = aber. “wacker” here is the older sense — brisk, wide-awake, spirited — not the modern “brave.” “holp” = half (halp), 3rd sg. past of helpen (helfen) — Grimm gloss it in the text with the parenthetical “(half),” reproduced as printed. “flietig” = fleißig; “drog” = trug; “auck” = auch; “Hus” = Haus.

sentences.t: dann was et awerst, eh en Augenschlägsken (Augenblick) vergienk, verswunnen.
sentences.l: but then it was, however, before a little moment (moment) passed by, vanished.
sentences.i: but then, before a moment’s glance had passed, it was gone.
sentences.n: “Augenschlägsken” — literally a “little eye-blink,” a diminutive; the Grimms gloss it in the text as “(Augenblick)” — the standard word for “moment.” The gloss is their own; reproduced exactly. “vergienk” = verging (past of vergehen). “verswunnen” = verschwunden — the missing High German consonant shift (Low German sw- for High German schw-) shows through.

sentences.t: Dat Kind vertelde et siner Moder, de wul et awerst nig glöven.
sentences.l: The child told it to its mother, but she would not believe it.
sentences.i: The child told her mother about it, but she would not believe it.
sentences.n: “vertelde” = erzählte (told). “siner Moder” = seiner Mutter. “nig” = nicht — a stock Low German form. “glöven” = glauben; the -v- for High German -b- is regular. “wul … nig glöven” = wollte … nicht glauben; here “wul” is “wollte” (past of wollen), not the flavor particle “wohl.”

sentences.t: Up et lest brochte et en Rause (Rose) mit un vertelde dat schöne Kind hädde em deise Rause gieven un hädde em sägt wenn de Rause upblöhet wär, dann wull et wier kummen.
sentences.l: At the last she brought a rose (rose) along with her, and told [her mother] the beautiful child had given her this rose, and had said to her, when the rose bloomed open, then it would come again.
sentences.i: At last she brought a rose home with her, and told her mother the beautiful child had given her this rose and had said that when the rose bloomed she would come back again.
sentences.n: “Up et lest” = aufs Letzte — at last, finally. “brochte” = brachte; “Rause” = Rose — Grimm gloss it in the text with “(Rose),” their own; reproduced as printed. “deise” = diese. “gieven” = geben (past participle gegeben; here “hädde gieven” = hätte gegeben, past subjunctive of reported speech). “sägt” = gesagt. “upblöhet” = aufgeblüht (bloomed open); the separable up- is Low German auf-. “wull … kummen” = wollte … kommen; “wier” = wieder. Square brackets in l supply the addressee (“her mother”) that the German leaves implicit.

sentences.t: De Moder stellde dei Rause in’t Water.
sentences.l: The mother placed the rose in the water.
sentences.n: “stellde” = stellte (placed upright, as one stands a stem in a vase). Watch “dei” here: in this tale it is the feminine accusative article “die” (Rause is feminine), not the past tense of any verb. “in’t” is Low German for in dat = in das — the ’t enclitic is a regular Low German shortening. “Water” = Wasser: the missing High German consonant shift (t for ss) is characteristic of Low German.

sentences.t: Einen Morgen kam dat Kind gar nig ut dem Bedde, de Moder gink to dem Bedde hen un fund dat Kind daude (todt); et lag awerst ganz anmotik.
sentences.l: One morning the child did not come out of bed at all; the mother went thither to the bed and found the child dead (dead); it lay, however, quite peaceful.
sentences.i: One morning the child would not come out of bed at all; the mother went over to the bed and found the child dead; but it lay there quite peaceful.
sentences.n: “ut dem Bedde” = aus dem Bette. “gink … hen” = ging … hin (thither). “fund” = fand (past of finnen / finden). “daude” = tot; Grimm gloss it in the text as “(todt)” — the 1857 High German spelling — and the gloss is their own, reproduced as printed. “anmotik” is a hapax here, a Low German adjective meaning “peaceful, gentle, calm-looking”; the sense is arguable and readers of Low German have taken it as “sweetly, gently” or “peaceful in appearance.” We render it plainly.

sentences.t: Un de Rause was den sulftigen Morgen upblöhet.
sentences.l: And the rose had bloomed open that same morning.
sentences.n: “sulftigen” = selbigen (self-same, that same); a Low German form of an already old High German pronoun. “upblöhet” = aufgeblüht (bloomed open). “was … upblöhet” — the perfect with the auxiliary sein, standard for verbs of change of state; here it reads as a past perfect against the preceding morning.

glossary.dei: die — the (fem. acc.; Low German = High German die; here 'dei Rause' = die Rose)
glossary.holt: das Holt — wood, firewood (Low German noun; = High German das Holz)
glossary.olle: alle — all, every (Low German; 'olle Dage' = alle Tage, every day)
glossary.t: dat / das — the (reduced enclitic article; Low German 'in't Water' = in dat Water = in das Wasser)
glossary.wul: wollen — would, wanted (3rd sg. past; Low German wul = High German wollte)
